item.title: Why the immediate future of liquid cooling is hybrid
item.description: From training massive language models to powering nonstop inference , AI is fundamentally rewriting the rules of data center thermal management. AI workloads are characteristically less predictable and significantly more power-dense than traditional operations. As a result, deploying liquid cooling is no longer an experimental consideration. It has become absolute table stakes for handling AI and high-performance computing (HPC) demands. The industry conversation has shifted rapidly from “if or when” to how quickly organizations can deploy and scale. Here is a look at how AI is driving the shift toward high-density thermal management , the operational realities of adopting these systems, why the near future belongs to hybrid environments, and how data center operators can successfully navigate the transition. AI Workloads Push Densities Beyond Air Alone: The Hybrid Era Historically, traditional cooling methods were sufficient for enterprise workloads. However, air cooling remains viable and efficient only up to approximately 20 to 40 kW per rack. Today’s GPU-accelerated AI racks commonly operate between 40 kW and well over 100 kW, with next-generation systems expected to push toward 200 kW or more. This GPU-driven density has made air-only cooling strategies fundamentally impractical for cutting-edge infrastructure. This extreme concentration of heat generation challenges traditional airflow-based architectures, demanding a transformation in AI data center cooling. In the ongoing evaluation of DLC vs. air (direct liquid cooling versus air cooling), t he performance data is conclusive . Thermal modeling demonstrates that single-phase direct liquid cooling maintains chip-to-coolant temperature differences of roughly 17 to 20 °C under roughly 500 W processor loads , whereas comparable air-cooled systems exceed 60 °C. Liquid cooling, which is up to 3,000 times more effective at transferring heat than air, efficiently captures heat directly at the source, preventing thermal throttling and protecting infrastructure ROI. While transitioning to liquid cooling may seem like a straightforward solution, it is rarely a sudden, wholesale replacement. Most facilities are not going all-in on liquid. Instead, they are adopting hybrid cooling models that combine traditional air architectures with advanced direct-to-chip systems. Why Hybrid Will Dominate Transitions Through 2027-2028 Through 2027 and 2028, hybrid thermal strategies will dominate because data centers must accommodate both legacy IT equipment and next-generation AI accelerators within the same facility. The reality of brownfield retrofits, where most AI capacity is initially being deployed in existing air-cooled facilities, versus designing greenfield sites for liquid from day one means that air cooling will still play a critical role in ancillary systems and lower-density zones. The future is not strictly liquid cooling only. It is about right-sizing the cooling method to the specific workload. Ope
item.dc:creator: Andrew Bradner
item.content:encoded: From training massive language models to powering nonstop inference , AI is fundamentally rewriting the rules of data center thermal management. AI workloads are characteristically less predictable and significantly more power-dense than traditional operations. As a result, deploying liquid cooling is no longer an experimental consideration. It has become absolute table stakes for handling AI and high-performance computing (HPC) demands. The industry conversation has shifted rapidly from “if or when” to how quickly organizations can deploy and scale. Here is a look at how AI is driving the shift toward high-density thermal management , the operational realities of adopting these systems, why the near future belongs to hybrid environments, and how data center operators can successfully navigate the transition. AI Workloads Push Densities Beyond Air Alone: The Hybrid Era Historically, traditional cooling methods were sufficient for enterprise workloads. However, air cooling remains viable and efficient only up to approximately 20 to 40 kW per rack. Today’s GPU-accelerated AI racks commonly operate between 40 kW and well over 100 kW, with next-generation systems expected to push toward 200 kW or more. This GPU-driven density has made air-only cooling strategies fundamentally impractical for cutting-edge infrastructure. This extreme concentration of heat generation challenges traditional airflow-based architectures, demanding a transformation in AI data center cooling. In the ongoing evaluation of DLC vs. air (direct liquid cooling versus air cooling), t he performance data is conclusive . Thermal modeling demonstrates that single-phase direct liquid cooling maintains chip-to-coolant temperature differences of roughly 17 to 20 °C under roughly 500 W processor loads , whereas comparable air-cooled systems exceed 60 °C. Liquid cooling, which is up to 3,000 times more effective at transferring heat than air, efficiently captures heat directly at the source, preventing thermal throttling and protecting infrastructure ROI. While transitioning to liquid cooling may seem like a straightforward solution, it is rarely a sudden, wholesale replacement. Most facilities are not going all-in on liquid. Instead, they are adopting hybrid cooling models that combine traditional air architectures with advanced direct-to-chip systems. Why Hybrid Will Dominate Transitions Through 2027-2028 Through 2027 and 2028, hybrid thermal strategies will dominate because data centers must accommodate both legacy IT equipment and next-generation AI accelerators within the same facility. The reality of brownfield retrofits, where most AI capacity is initially being deployed in existing air-cooled facilities, versus designing greenfield sites for liquid from day one means that air cooling will still play a critical role in ancillary systems and lower-density zones. The future is not strictly liquid cooling only. It is about right-sizing the cooling method to the specific workload. Operators will successfully scale by deploying mixed architectures, such as utilizing direct-to-chip cold plates and Coolant Distribution Units (CDUs) for dense AI clusters, while managing residual heat with Computer Room Air Handlers (CRAHs) or fan-assisted Rear-Door Heat Exchangers (RDHx). The Real Bottleneck: Operational Complexity and the Talent Gap While the technology for liquid cooling is maturing, navigating the operational complexity of a hybrid cooling environment is the real challenge. Cooling is no longer just a facilities issue. It requires the convergence of IT, mechanical engineering, and software management. Facilities must now manage fluid chemistry, leak detection, risk mitigation, and sophisticated maintenance workflows. What’s more, the industry is facing a widening talent gap. Uptime Institute reports that nearly two-thirds of operators struggle to hire and retain qualified staff, underscoring a shortage of teams with expertise across both liquid cooling systems and integrated infrastructure. Addressing this will require new training models, deeper vendor collaboration, and greater reliance on managed services. While the industry is making strides toward standardizing interoperable designs - such as plug-and-play CDUs and manifolds that distribute coolant efficiently across racks - there is still fragmentation across vendors and approaches. Additionally, operators must navigate changing economics. While liquid infrastructure requires higher upfront CapEx, it delivers better Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) over time due to enhanced efficiency and density. Decision-makers are consequently shifting their focus from what is cheapest today to what can scale with AI demand. A Blueprint for Success: Reference Architectures and Readiness Navigating this hybrid cooling transition requires standardizing deployments to avoid complex, bespoke engineering for every site. A successful liquid cooling ecosystem relies on selecting the appropriate heat rejection architectures, which are defined by the heat capture method, CDU type (rack-mounted or floor-mounted), and the method of rejecting heat outdoors. A successful blueprint involve s choosing among six core architectures, ranging from rejecting heat to air within the IT space via liquid-to-air (L-A) CDUs, to utilizing dedicated independent water systems with liquid-to-liquid (L-L) CDUs for massive deployments. To future-proof AI infrastructure, operators should utilize a strategic readiness checklist: ● Plan in Parallel: Physical infrastructure and IT planning must happen simultaneously from day one to prevent facilities from lagging behind hardware deployments. ● Design for Flexibility: Build dynamic, responsive designs capable of supporting multiple hardware generations, utilizing hybrid air and liquid combinations. ● Embrace Sustainability and Heat Reuse: Tying cooling strategies to ESG goals is a clear win, as advanced liquid cooling solutions can reduce total facility energy consumption by up to 40 percent and cut water use by 20-90 percent. Furthermore, liquid cooling unlocks opportunities for heat reuse, allowing operators to redirect waste heat to adjacent buildings or district heating systems. Derisking Adoption Through Integrated Partnerships Deploying liquid cooling at scale introduces risk, particularly when sourcing racks, power, and cooling from multiple uncoordinated vendors. To derisk adoption and bridge the talent gap, operators must lean on integrated, end-to-end partnerships. Providers like Schneider Electric are addressing this complexity by engineering fully synchronized ecosystems. Facilities can successfully derisk liquid cooling transitions by focusing on: ● Integrated Power and Cooling: At AI densities, even minor imbalances between electrical load and thermal rejection can lead to system instability, underscoring the necessity of integrated AI data center cooling solutions. Through its acquisition of Motivair, Schneider Electric now offers a complete end-to-end liquid cooling ecosystem (including CDUs, cold plates, and manifolds) that is designed to work seamlessly alongside resilient uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and distribution units. ● Validated Designs: Collaborating early with IT vendors and chip designers helps align reference designs for optimized integration. For example, Schneider Electric’s close collaboration with NVIDIA on validated architectures helps prevent physical infrastructure from becoming a bottleneck to GPU performance. ● Digital Lifecycle Management: AI infrastructure must become more dynamic. Using digital twins and simulation software, like Schneider Electric’s ETAP and AVEVA platforms, teams can design, model, and validate integrated power and cooling architectures before physical construction begins, predicting issues before they arise. ● Global Manufacturing and Services: Sourcing from partners with robust global manufacturing capacity reduces supply chain risk and accel

item.title: Shola Ameobi: ‘I thought: how can I be most useful to Newcastle? Then the cog started turning’
item.description: From experiencing racism growing up in Newcastle to becoming a derby hero and now a member of the executive team, the former striker has been on a remarkable journey “There were times where I feared for my life as a kid, being harassed and chased by different groups of people,” Shola Ameobi says. “There were situations where I had to sprint to get away from groups of lads who didn’t like me because of what I looked like.” Ameobi is recalling growing up in Newcastle during the late 1980s and 1990s, having moved from Nigeria aged six. There were lots of moments like that. Continue reading...

item.title: Certification authority eMudhra defends its laughably weak private keys
item.description: Indian certification authority eMudhra has defended the laughably weak private keys it used to sign some digital certificates it issued, and suggested others should share the blame for the incident. In case you’re coming to this one late, news broke yesterday that private keys the company used to sign certs were beyond weak: one was literally just the number “4,” and several others were short strings of easily guessed two-or-three-digit numbers. It’s easy to deduce the value of those keys, which makes it possible to forge certs and impersonate websites or other resources. That’s gold for scammers, phishers, and other miscreants. The entire infosec industry has pointed that out, urged swift adoption of better certs, and lamented the fact that implementing replacements will be a long and thankless task. eMudhra’s statement about the incident says it generated keys during “a Key Generation Ceremony (KGC) held on April 30, 2025, using FIPS 140-2 Level 3 Hardware Security Modules (HSMs).” Such hardware is the standard kit for the job and should in theory produce nicely complex keys and store them securely. But something went wrong. “A flaw in the KGC caused a wrap/unwrap step to produce a second set of weak keys alongside the original strong keys,” the statement claims. “The weak keys were the ones published to the browser root stores. eMudhra is working to establish the root cause.” The company then gets a tad defensive. “These roots and issuing CAs have gone through independent audits for two years in a row and have been in browser trust lists since mid-2025,” the statement adds, seemingly shifting some blame to auditors and other stakeholders. The announcement then points out that eMudhra’s TLS business generates just one percent of its revenue, meaning this mess won’t impact its bottom line too much. That’s nice to know for the company’s investors but rather misses the point that whoever relies on the company now has an urgent, unwanted, and costly job to do replacing certs. “eMudhra is working directly with customers who may be affected to give them replacement certificates, so that critical services are not disrupted. The company is also working with the root programs and continues its root-cause investigation,” the statement adds. The company allows that the incident “may have some reputational risks on eMudhra which cannot be quantified.” Ya think? ®

item.title: AI firms say UK has a year to head off datacentre protests before construction is threatened
item.description: Exclusive: Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco taskforce urges ministers to offer areas greater benefits from tech infrastructure amid fears of US-style opposition AI companies have told ministers they have 12 months to head off public opposition to datacentres in the UK or risk US-style protests that could threaten their construction. Successive dry summers and rising energy bills are increasing public scrutiny of plans for the huge computer warehouses that are used to train and run AI models, says a submission to the Labour government from a group including the AI infrastructure companies Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco. Continue reading...

item.title: IBM CEO says open weight models are now irresistibly good and cheap on-prem
item.description: IBM CEO Arvind Krishna has told investors that open weight models now make brilliant sense for on-prem enterprise use. Speaking on the company’s Q3 earnings call, Krishna said that in 2024 closed frontier models were plainly superior to open alternatives. “If you ran some assessment, some benchmark, and it was broad-based, not narrow, the top model might score a 70, and the open model might score a 20 or a 30.” “In late 2025, we began to see that gap shrink, where maybe the gap was not 70 to 20 or 30, it was 70 to 50,” he continued. The CEO said open weight models currently deliver “anywhere from 25 percent to 10 percent of the token cost of the frontier models. That is very attractive given that they’re now 90 percent as effective.” “It’s a simple question for any enterprise. Would you like something that’s 10 percent of the cost if it’s 90 percent as good as the best, or do you want to pay that 10 times higher cost?” Krishna thinks businesses will most often choose not to incur the higher costs. “Then the question is: how many tasks require that? I would tell you some do, but the vast majority, summarizing an email, examining a contract, answering a customer call, composing an email, all of those can be done as well with the much cheaper answer.” The CEO said those numbers mean IBM is seeing booming interest in on-prem AI infrastructure. While he thinks most businesses can build useful AI infrastructure in just two or three racks, he feels many will struggle to get it running. “The question becomes: how do you do that?” he said. “The question that the enterprise struggles with is: ‘Where are my kernel engineers? Where are the people who worry about the underlying network? Who can make sure that the model is clustered on GPUs that are close to each other in network proximity? Who can make sure that you’re doing the right caching of results so you get an incredible response?’” He didn’t have answers, other than to say IBM will produce software that eases AI deployments. Krishna also predicted demand for on-prem AI will spur sales of Big Blue’s Spyre mainframe accelerator cards. The CEO said current-gen z17 mainframes have delivered $1bn more revenue than any previous model, and said Big Blue’s new rackable models delivered “the strongest midrange launch in IBM Z in nearly two decades.” Mainframe revenue, however, fell 20 percent – as IBM expects given it’s now 18 months since it launched the z17. IBM’s infrastructure revenue grew five percent year-over-year to $3.7 billion, much slower improvement than recorded by rivals Dell, HPE, and Lenovo. Software did rather better, scoring nine percent growth to reach $7.8 billion for the quarter. Red Hat was the star, growing eleven percent and increasing annual recurring revenue by 30 percent. Some of that future revenue is for Red Hat’s virtualization products, which have now won $800 million of deals, with a pipeline of a further $750 million. Where are the people who worry about the underlying network? Who can make sure that the model is clustered on GPUs that are close to each other in network proximity? Who can make sure that you’re doing the right caching of results so you get an incredible response?’” He didn’t have answers, other than to say IBM will produce software that eases AI deployments. Krishna also predicted demand for on-prem AI will spur sales of Big Blue’s Spyre mainframe accelerator cards. IBM’s infrastructure revenue grew five percent year-over-year to $3.7 billion, much slower improvement than recorded by rivals Dell, HPE, and Lenovo. Software did rather better, scoring nine percent growth to reach $7.8 billion for the quarter. Red Hat was the star, growing eleven percent and increasing annual recurring revenue by 30 percent. Some of that future revenue is for Red Hat’s virtualization products, which have now won $800 million of deals, with a pipeline of a further $750 million. That’s a solid result for a product line launched in 2024, and IBM believes there’s more to come given the possibility some VMware users are on the move. Total quarterly revenue hit $17.1 billion, up five percent. IBM’s share price wobbled in after-hours trading and ended down a point or two. ‘Emergency maintenance’ for IBM Cloud Another IBM matter The Register is watching today is a severity one incident in the Big Blue cloud, caused by “emergency maintenance” that meant users could not provision new resources or virtual private clouds for 90 minutes. Users of IBM’s Classic Cloud, the service it acquired from SoftLayer in 2013, have been told Big Blue will “restore new provisioning and resource management in our Classic environment” by 08:00 UTC on Thursday – meaning the incident will last at least 16 hours. IBM commenced that work a handful of hours after the announcement of critical bugs in PHP . We’ve asked if fixing that flaw is the reason for the incident and will update this story if we get a response. ®

item.title: APOD: 2026 October 22 – The First Green Star, WD J1330+6435
item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 October 22 – The… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. The First Green Star, WD J1330+6435 Explanation: Star light, star bright: is there a green star out tonight? Other than the Sun , all stars are so far from Earth that they appear as points in the sky. They are mostly white, but sometimes noticeably red or blue . This color typically relates to the temperature: blue stars are hotter than red stars. What about other colors? The featured image is an illustration showing WD J1330+6435 , a white dwarf star , surrounded by an accretion disk with gas and rocks orbiting the star. White dwarfs are small, faint stars that are left over when a star like the Sun exhausts its nuclear fuel . Astronomers recently found that some white dwarf stars, despite their name, would appear yellow, green, cyan, pink, or purple . In these cases , trace elements that were accreted to these stars interact with the stellar atmosphere and shift its normally white color. But, alas! I wish I may, I wish I might, but they are too faint to see tonight … Tomorrow’s picture: eye in the sky Date October 22, 2026 Credit & Copyright Mark A. item.title: Fires Char New Guinea
item.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Fires Char New Guinea Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search New Guinea, the world’s second-largest island, harbors an extraordinary variety of plant life across more than a dozen distinct ecoregions , including seasonally dry savannas, tropical rainforests, and lowland swamp forests. But in September and October 2026, as drought gripped New Guinea (sometimes called Papua) amid a strong El Niño , fires scorched the island and smoke shrouded large swaths of it for weeks. The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-20 satellite captured this image of thick smoke streaming from the southern part of the island on October 11, 2026. In recent weeks, soaring levels of air pollution delayed and canceled flights , closed schools, and prompted officials in some areas to urge children and older people to wear masks. “Sometimes smoke that has drifted into the convection of nearby thunderstorms will get washed out or lofted up into the upper troposphere, but a lot of smoke stays near the surface and causes air quality problems,” said Robert Field, an associate research scientist at NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies and Columbia University. “It’s a horrible situation.” According to the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED), a fire emissions monitoring system, fires in Papua New Guinea, on the eastern half of the island, had released nearly 32 megatons of carbon by October 17, more than any other year on record at that point in the year (charts above). “Emissions are already much higher than the 2015 total for the year, and it’s very likely that this will become the highest year on record for Papua New Guinea, even surpassing 1997,” said Guido van der Werf, a fire scientist at Wageningen University & Research. On the Indonesian side, sometimes called West New Guinea or Indonesian Papua, carbon emissions exceeded 35 megatons , the third highest after 2015 and 1997, other El Niño years with severe fires. Van der Werf led the development of GFED, a satellite-driven modeling framework that uses a mix of remote sensing , vegetation characteristics, and other information to estimate the extent of vegetation fires and the emissions over nearly three decades. But in September and October 2026, as drought gripped New Guinea (sometimes called Papua) amid a strong El Niño , fires scorched the island and smoke shrouded large swaths of it for weeks. The VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite) on the NOAA-20 satellite captured this image of thick smoke streaming from the southern part of the island on October 11, 2026. In recent weeks, soaring levels of air pollution delayed and canceled flights , closed schools, and prompted officials in some areas to urge children and older people to wear masks. “Sometimes smoke that has drifted into the convection of nearby thunderstorms will get washed out or lofted up into the upper troposphere, but a lot of smoke stays near the surface and causes air quality problems,” said Robert Field, an associate research scientist at NASA’s Goddard Institute for Space Studies and Columbia University. “It’s a horrible situation.” According to the Global Fire Emissions Database (GFED), a fire emissions monitoring system, fires in Papua New Guinea, on the eastern half of the island, had released nearly 32 megatons of carbon by October 17, more than any other year on record at that point in the year (charts above). “Emissions are already much higher than the 2015 total for the year, and it’s very likely that this will become the highest year on record for Papua New Guinea, even surpassing 1997,” said Guido van der Werf, a fire scientist at Wageningen University & Research. On the Indonesian side, sometimes called West New Guinea or Indonesian Papua, carbon emissions exceeded 35 megatons , the third highest after 2015 and 1997, other El Niño years with severe fires. Van der Werf led the development of GFED, a satellite-driven modeling framework that uses a mix of remote sensing , vegetation characteristics, and other information to estimate the extent of vegetation fires and the emissions over nearly three decades. Unusually dry weather—a byproduct of El Niño shifting rainfall patterns —has primed ecosystems across the island to burn. The southernmost part of Papua New Guinea, dominated by relatively fire-prone savannas and grasslands of the Trans-Fly region , went more than 90 consecutive days without rain, according to Papua New Guinea’s National Weather Service . Since August, parts of the region have seen precipitation of roughly 5 to 10 percent of normal, according to the weather service’s data. Local news outlets report that drought is causing crop failures , water shortages , and school disruptions . In this normally wet part of the world, people ignite the vast majority of fires, researchers say. Crop fires, pasture maintenance, deforestation and land clearing, and hunting are all common reasons people burn in New Guinea. In dry conditions, managed fires sometimes spread and burn uncontrolled as wildfires, particularly in the drier, southernmost parts of the island. “We’re seeing an exceptionally high level of fire activity in Papua New Guinea and Eastern Indonesia, particularly Indonesian Papua and Kalimantan, this year compared with Sumatra and other parts of Western Indonesia,” said Yang Chen, an associate researcher at the University of California, Irvine. “Papua has emerged as Indonesia’s new deforestation frontier.” Over the past two decades , land in Indonesian Papua has been cleared for industrial oil palm and pulpwood plantations, shifting small-scale cultivation, urban expansion, and mining . According to Global Forest Watch, the region lost 27,000 hectares of primary forest in 2025, nearly double the 2024 total and the most since 2017. Sumatra’s fires are relatively low compared to other drought years partly because many areas are already developed. “Areas with large oil palm, sugarcane, or pulpwood plantations also often have their own private fire brigades to protect their assets,” said Field. “It’s in unmanaged areas or primary forest edges where we’re generally seeing the most fire.” Researchers expect the fires to continue until the heavy rains of the wet season arrive in the southern part of New Guinea, typically in early November. item.title: Philippine government suspends top tech official for alleged misconduct
item.description: The Philippines government’s Ombudsman has suspended a senior Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) official over allegations he assigned government contracts to a company he founded and continued to hold a stake in. The Ombudsman announced the suspension yesterday and named Undersecretary for E-Government David L. Almirol as the individual of concern, after considering “administrative complaints of Grave Misconduct, Conduct Prejudicial to the Best Interest of the Service and violation of … the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees.” “In ordering the preventive suspension, the Ombudsman found strong evidence supporting the administrative charges against Almirol,” according to its announcement of the suspension. Almirol founded a company called Multisys Technologies Corporation that offers software development services, plus packaged products. After over a decade as the company’s CEO, Almirol in 2022 joined DICT at the request of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., to work on improving e-government services. The Ombudsman alleged that between 2023 and 2025 DICT awarded at least eight contracts valued at over ₱1.5 billion ($24 million) to entities linked with Multisys. The contracts covered information and communications technology consultancy, e-government application deployment, web-based messaging services, cloud infrastructure, data center colocation and software subscriptions. Evidence of those transactions is apparently on the record in Multisys’s books. Local laws mean Almirol should have divested his stake in Multisys within 60 days. The Ombudsman alleges the exec missed that deadline but later complied. It’s not alleged he issued contracts in the period during which he continued to hold Multisys shares. The Ombudsman has suspended Almirol without pay for six months, a step it says is necessary because if he continued in the role it “could prejudice the investigation, particularly given his control and custody of documents and evidence relevant to the case.” The org has also pointed out that its decision does not pre-judge the matter, but is “a precautionary measure intended to preserve the integrity of the proceedings and ensure an impartial and unimpeded investigation.” President Marcos Jr. made rooting out corruption a key plank of his platform and even created an agency to tackle the problem. However, it’s felt that some anti-corruption actions may have been partly politically motivated. Past tech-related scandals in the Philippines include a 2022 case that saw its Department of Education overpay for lousy laptops . ®

item.title: Canadian publisher Boréal ends relationship with novelist Thélyson Orélien over alleged use of AI
item.description: Author withdrawn from France’s Prix Goncourt last month has repeatedly denied using artificial intelligence to write novel The publisher of top-selling Haitian Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien, who was removed from France’s most prestigious literary prize list last month, has confirmed the author used artificial intelligence to help write his novel C’était ça ou mourir (It Was Either That or Die). Orélien has denied allegations that he used AI on his breakthrough novel and, last week, Canadian publisher Les Éditions du Boréal said it was standing by the 38-year-old writer. Continue reading...

item.title: To help world gorge on GPUs, Nvidia brings cash bucket to fatten wafer-thin supply chain
item.description: Nvidia has decided that its future prospects rest on an improved silicon substrate and packing supply chain, so has dipped into its giant pile of cash to ensure it can get the parts it needs by ensuring its suppliers have the resources needed to play their small part in keeping the flow of GPUs and AI processors strong. It’s not unusual for manufacturers to invest in their suppliers, because it helps to create certainty and spread financial risk. For those deals to be announced at a major tech company’s conference – as Nvidia did at its Berlin GTC gabfest – is somewhat novel, suggesting the company feels the need to show investors it is working to ensure it can meet demand for its products, and that demand will persist for years. Several of Nvidia’s announcements pertained to silicon substrates, aka wafers. Whatever you call them, they’re blank, round, silicon slabs onto which chipmakers etch circuits. They’re made by companies that sell to foundries like TSMC and Intel, which then turn them into chips of various flavours. At GTC Berlin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang observed that demand for AI hardware is vast, but that “Capacity is the constraint.” Specifically, capacity for activities like building substrates, advanced silicon packaging, testing, and creating optical connectors. Big Green therefore plans to increase substrate capacity for its products by 2.5x over the next three years. To make that happen, Nvidia has added Samsung’s Electro-Mechanics business unit to its substrate supply chain. Samsung apparently has immediate capacity at a factory in South Korea and Nvidia intends to tap that now. The deal means that by 2028, about a quarter of Sammy’s substrate output will go to Nvidia. Nvidia already has a deal with Japanese substrate outfit IBIDEN. In Berlin, the GPU giant pointed to further expansion that will triple production at an IBIDEN plant. Taiwanese substrate player Unimicron is also benefiting from Nvidia’s generosity, in the form of a capacity reservation agreement and associated plant expansion plans. It’s not just wafers that Nvidia wants to tuck into. The company has also signed a capacity reservation with Korean silicon packaging player Amkor. Again, Big Green’s involvement will see its partner expand capacity, in this case by 300 percent. Nvidia says this deal “will support higher production volumes for current and next-generation platforms.” AI systems need speedy networks, and many players see optical connections as the best way to build systems capable of handling the data deluges modern workloads create and require. Nvidia has therefore hatched a plan to boost manufacturing capacity at optics outfit SPIL. Again, Big Green already has a deal with the company, but in Berlin it expanded that arrangement in the hope it expands production capacity 15x by mid-2027, then doubles that again by the end of 2028. All of which suggests that Nvidia believes the AI infrastructure boom has years left to run. ®

item.title: PHP blames supply chain security biz Chainguard for putting huge chunks of the web at risk
item.description: PHP developers have accused software supply chain security shop Chainguard of effectively revealing critical bugs in the open-source scripting language ahead of a planned official disclosure. On Wednesday, just hours after releasing emergency patches for the two bugs collectively called PHP2shell, PHP maintainers published a blog about how the vulnerabilities were found and fixed. They credited researchers at Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz with finding the security holes between August and September. All three companies have said they used AI models to find the vulnerabilities, which are now tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on servers running PHP. This is especially serious because PHP powers huge chunks of the public web. It also adds a dose of irony to the “leak and disrupted disclosure” part of the blog, which blames Chainguard - a company that aims to secure software supply chains by hardening open source code - for the messy disclosure. The trouble, according to PHP developers, started on Tuesday around 15:00 UTC, when “two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media,” along with incorrect information about the release time and CVSS severity rating. At that point, no technical details leaked. The rumors, however, prompted PHP maintainers to warn people in advance about the critical flaws, and move the planned disclosure forward a day, from Thursday to Wednesday. “Distributors were still packaging the fix, so releasing immediately would have left many users without an easy way to update,” the PHP Foundation blog says. “Moving the release forward by one day was the best compromise between acting quickly, giving people time to prepare, and making sure everyone had a simple update path when the vulnerabilities were disclosed.” A couple of hours later, Calif “mistakenly” published a video showing a proof-of-concept exploit and “additional, though limited” information about the bugs, we’re told. “Mitigation advice we started providing to a few critical infrastructure providers around Oct 20th 23:00 UTC, may have leaked as well,” the PHP blog says, but it does not name these providers. And then it throws Chainguard under the bus: “On October 21st at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the coordinated release, Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix. Like other distributors, Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure.” Chainguard CEO: 'We made the call' Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc spoke with The Register on Wednesday, and while he doesn’t dispute the timeline, said his company "didn't leak." “These things are messy,” Lorenc said. Chainguard learned “something
item.dc:creator: Jessica Lyons
item.content:encoded: PHP developers have accused software supply chain security shop Chainguard of effectively revealing critical bugs in the open-source scripting language ahead of a planned official disclosure. On Wednesday, just hours after releasing emergency patches for the two bugs collectively called PHP2shell, PHP maintainers published a blog about how the vulnerabilities were found and fixed. They credited researchers at Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz with finding the security holes between August and September. All three companies have said they used AI models to find the vulnerabilities, which are now tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on servers running PHP. This is especially serious because PHP powers huge chunks of the public web. It also adds a dose of irony to the “leak and disrupted disclosure” part of the blog, which blames Chainguard - a company that aims to secure software supply chains by hardening open source code - for the messy disclosure. The trouble, according to PHP developers, started on Tuesday around 15:00 UTC, when “two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media,” along with incorrect information about the release time and CVSS severity rating. At that point, no technical details leaked. The rumors, however, prompted PHP maintainers to warn people in advance about the critical flaws, and move the planned disclosure forward a day, from Thursday to Wednesday. “Distributors were still packaging the fix, so releasing immediately would have left many users without an easy way to update,” the PHP Foundation blog says. “Moving the release forward by one day was the best compromise between acting quickly, giving people time to prepare, and making sure everyone had a simple update path when the vulnerabilities were disclosed.” A couple of hours later, Calif “mistakenly” published a video showing a proof-of-concept exploit and “additional, though limited” information about the bugs, we’re told. “Mitigation advice we started providing to a few critical infrastructure providers around Oct 20th 23:00 UTC, may have leaked as well,” the PHP blog says, but it does not name these providers. And then it throws Chainguard under the bus: “On October 21st at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the coordinated release, Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix. Like other distributors, Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure.” Chainguard CEO: 'We made the call' Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc spoke with The Register on Wednesday, and while he doesn’t dispute the timeline, said his company "didn't leak." “These things are messy,” Lorenc said. Chainguard learned “something was coming in PHP” on Friday from one of the researchers that found the bugs, Lorenc told us. Later that night, using his company’s AI harness and a frontier model, the CEO and the Chainguard team independently found the same memory corruption vulnerabilities. All it took was a “basic prompt of ‘find bad vulnerabilities in PHP,’” Lorenc wrote in a subsequent LinkedIn post. On Saturday, Chainguard began working with the PHP maintainers, confirmed that some of its findings matched the bug reports, and helped test the patches. “The patches are crazy - this is not a simple vulnerability,” Lorenc told The Register . “It really did take them months to build a real, working patch for it. And then on Monday, the rumors started, and yesterday it just spiraled.” Some people published POCs on social media, other security vendors reported seeing real-world exploitation, and late Tuesday night Lorenc told us he decided to ship the fixes, and notified the PHP coordinated disclosure channel about his plans. “People were getting hit in advance” of the official PHP disclosure, “so we made the call to ship the fixes under that,” Lorenc said. “It's coordinated vulnerability disclosure, unless there's evidence of active exploits in the wild.” Also on Tuesday night, Chainguard published built artifacts and made them accessible to anyone, not just customers. “And then I woke up this morning and saw that this was all our fault,” Lorenc said. When asked if he would do anything differently, given the fallout from Chainguard’s early disclosure, Lorenc said no. “This process and policy is based on trying to coordinate as much as possible until shit hits the fan and people start weaponizing things,” he said. “It sucks, because we really are all on one team, and there's bad guys over there doing stuff.” Chainguard’s honeypots trapped IPs from China and Russia targeting the vulnerabilities on Wednesday, Lorenc added. “Just being told there's a vulnerability in a piece of software - even something as big as PHP - is enough to find it,” he told us. “I did that myself without any other knowledge on Friday." "I think this is kind of the new normal. People are able to build an exploit in hours without even knowing what the vulnerability is." What we know about the CVEs and how to exploit them While we still don’t know the scope of exploitation - or what will happen to vulnerable legacy systems that don’t have security fixes - threat hunters predict it’s going to be a doozy. “Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them,” Wiz researchers Sagi Tzadik, Shir Tamari, Nir Ohfeld, and Tomer Schwartz warned on Wednesday, adding the oft-quoted stat that PHP powers 70 percent of all websites in the world. “Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4,” the Wiz kids wrote. “Attackers can exploit them remotely, in some cases fairly easily. Immediate patching is strongly advised.” Both bugs are related to how PHP handles memory management and error handling, and both lead to remote code execution (RCE). They can cause a corrupted internal PHP state when a request ends unexpectedly, and then a later request can reuse that state, leading to memory disclosure or RCE. “Both are memory corruption vulnerabilities,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity explained. “If an attacker can shape the memory PHP trusts, they can potentially hijack what it does next, and in these cases that means remote code execution.” CVE-2026-109618 ( GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w ) leads to RCE via out-of-memory corruption. “If a request reached PHP's memory_limit at exactly the wrong moment, PHP could leave partially initialized internal data behind and later treat it as valid, corrupting memory,” the project maintainer wrote. “On Apache with mod_php, an unauthenticated request can trigger this before any application code runs.” CVE-2026-109619 ( GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp ) allows RCE via stale state. “A fatal error at the wrong point could leave internal state pointing to memory that belonged to a previous request,” according to the PGP Foundation. “A later request handled by the same worker could then use that freed memory. A use-after-free and worker crash were confirmed, and the reporter demonstrated remote code execution against a real-world application running on Apache with mod_php.”®

item.title: FCC chair warns media not to run the "fake polls" Trump keeps complaining about
item.description: Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr today warned broadcasters about airing "fake polls," amplifying one of the many complaints that President Trump has regularly made about the news media. Carr's post on X said, "Many journalists and broadcasters have been amplifying or airing these Polls without regard to basic journalistic ethics and without informing the public that those Polls lack a scientific, accurate, or even real basis... Broadcasters are advised to avoid engaging in News Distortions or running Broadcast Hoaxes by airing Polls that would violate their regulatory obligations." Carr urged broadcasters to "provide their viewers with additional context and information about Polls they have covered." In fact, one small polling outfit was exposed as a hoax this week, and a similar incident occurred in August. News outlets have reported on these hoaxes, providing the very "context" that Carr said is needed. Read full article Comments

item.title: Broda Shaggi Reveals He Was Hit by a Stray Bullet in New Documentary
item.description: Samuel Animashaun Perry (Broda Shaggi) explains the stray bullet incident behind his months-long hiatus in a new video. If you are a fan of Broda Shaggi ‘s skits, his music, or even just his lively presence on your timelines, you must have noticed that the popular entertainer and actor has been noticeably absent from social media over the past few months. Samuel Animashaun Perry has now officially returned, bringing along a deeply moving mini-documentary that breaks his silence and reveals the terrifying life-threatening ordeal behind his sudden hiatus . The multi-AMVCA winner revealed that his unexpected break was caused by a horrific incident where he was struck by a stray bullet while returning from a shoot. Recounting the frightening moment, Broda Shaggi shared,”We were done shooting and were on our way when we got stuck in a holdup. Suddenly, I heard a loud bang and everywhere went silent. I could see people talking, but I couldn’t hear anything. Then I touched my hip and saw blood. That was when it dawned on me that I had been hit by a stray bullet.” Broda Shaggi in an eccentric futuristic costume for one of his signature video skits. The incident led to an emergency hospital admission, extensive medical procedures, and an intensive period of physical rehabilitation . For a performer whose entire craft relies on boundless physical energy, comedy, and stage presence, being bedridden and unable to move presented immense physical and emotional hurdles . In the video, he candidly reflects on the overwhelming fear of losing his mobility and the uncertainty of how he would continue doing what he loves . Tracing his road from severe setback to resurgence, the documentary shows his gradual process of learning to walk again, moving from complete immobility to crutches and eventually regaining his strength . Now stepping back in front of the camera on his own terms, Broda Shaggi is turning what could have been a tragic end into a triumphant second chapter, ready to reconnect with his fans and dive back into his creative work . Watch below The post Broda Shaggi Reveals He Was Hit by a Stray Bullet in New Documentary appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: On this day in space! Oct. 21, 2008: India launches its 1st mission to the moon with Chandrayaan-1
item.description: null On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. The mission was named Chandrayaan-1, and it consisted of both an orbiter and an impactor. Chandrayaan-1 launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Center on an Indian rocket called the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, or PSLV-XL. (Launch occurred at 8:52 p.m. EDT, though it was about 6:22 a.m. local time at the launch site on Oct. 22.) It arrived in lunar orbit about three weeks later and dropped off the Moon Impact Probe, which crashed into the moon on Nov. 14. The rest of the Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft stayed in orbit, where it collected and transmitted data from the moon to Earth for about a year. The mission ended abruptly 14 months ahead of its planned end date when scientists lost contact with the probe . An Indian PSLV rocket launches the Chandrayaan-1 moon mission on Oct. 21, 2008 EDT (Oct. 22 local time in India). (Image credit: ISRO) Why it mattered The Indian Space Research Organisation , or ISRO, had a lot riding on the success of Chandrayaan-1 moon mission, which marked the first-ever deep space mission by the Indian space agency. It was also the first mission to the moon for India, a country that hopes to launch its own crewed spacecraft and build a space station. Chandrayaan-1 did more than just demonstrate that India's space program was capable of launching missions to the moon; it also returned some amazing science results, like evidence of water ice on the moon . "In September 2009, scientists published results of data collected by the American M3 instrument which had detected absorption features on the polar regions of the surface of the Moon usually linked to hydroxyl- and/ or water-bearing molecules," NASA said in a mission overview . The spacecraft carried 11 instruments to study the moon, five of them built by ISRO. The rest were experiments for the European Space Agnecy and NASA. "In addition to the five Indian instruments, the spacecraft carried scientific equipment from the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Sweden, and Bulgaria," NASA said. item.dc:creator: Hanneke Weitering
item.content:encoded: null On Oct. 21, 2008, the Indian Space Research Organization launched its first mission to the moon. The mission was named Chandrayaan-1, and it consisted of both an orbiter and an impactor. Chandrayaan-1 launched from the Satish Dhawan Space Center on an Indian rocket called the Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle, or PSLV-XL. (Launch occurred at 8:52 p.m. EDT, though it was about 6:22 a.m. local time at the launch site on Oct. 22.) It arrived in lunar orbit about three weeks later and dropped off the Moon Impact Probe, which crashed into the moon on Nov. 14. The rest of the Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft stayed in orbit, where it collected and transmitted data from the moon to Earth for about a year. The mission ended abruptly 14 months ahead of its planned end date when scientists lost contact with the probe . An Indian PSLV rocket launches the Chandrayaan-1 moon mission on Oct. 21, 2008 EDT (Oct. 22 local time in India). (Image credit: ISRO) Why it mattered The Indian Space Research Organisation , or ISRO, had a lot riding on the success of Chandrayaan-1 moon mission, which marked the first-ever deep space mission by the Indian space agency. It was also the first mission to the moon for India, a country that hopes to launch its own crewed spacecraft and build a space station. Chandrayaan-1 did more than just demonstrate that India's space program was capable of launching missions to the moon; it also returned some amazing science results, like evidence of water ice on the moon . "In September 2009, scientists published results of data collected by the American M3 instrument which had detected absorption features on the polar regions of the surface of the Moon usually linked to hydroxyl- and/ or water-bearing molecules," NASA said in a mission overview . The spacecraft carried 11 instruments to study the moon, five of them built by ISRO. The rest were experiments for the European Space Agnecy and NASA. "In addition to the five Indian instruments, the spacecraft carried scientific equipment from the United States, the United Kingdom, Germany, Sweden, and Bulgaria," NASA said. It took until Nov. 8, 2008 for Chandrayaan-1 to enter lunar orbit, where it stayed until contact was lost in August 2009, most likely due to a power supply failure caused by overheating. "This was short of the spacecraft’s planned two-year lifetime, although ISRO noted that at least 95% of its mission objectives had been accomplished by then," NASA wrote. NASA's Mini-SAR instrument, which flew aboard India's Chandrayaan-1 spacecraft, found more than 40 small craters with water ice. The craters range in size from 1 to 9 miles (2 to 15 km) in diameter. (Image credit: NASA) India did not stop at the moon with Chandrayaan-1. In 2019, the country launched the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter, which carried the Vikram lander and Pragyan rover. Chandrayaan-2 reached lunar orbit successfully, but the Vikram landing failed . The Chandrayaan-3 misson followed in 2023, which successfully landed a new Vikram lander and Pragyan rover near the moon's south pole. India plans to launch the Chandryaan-4 mission to return moon samples to Earth in 2028 . Want more space history? Check out our full On This Day In Space Story archive and watch our On This Day In Space videos on YouTube .

item.title: Olamide Wants Us to Party on “Burukutu” | Watch Video
item.description: Olamide releases his new single Burukutu alongside his upcoming album Time & Space. Photo Credit: Olamide/Instagram When the YBNL Nation boss decides to drop new music, the entire continent pauses to listen. Olamide is back in his absolute element, and the music community is buzzing following a major surprise release that has everyone talking. Building on the momentum of his previous self-titled album Olamidé released last year, the rap icon has dropped a brand-new single while officially setting the timeline for his next massive project. Olamide’s latest single is titled “ Burukutu ”. Named after the traditional, locally brewed fermented grain beverage found across various parts of Nigeria, the track leans heavily into street-level jubilation and celebratory culture, opening with the infectious chant, “Baddoo we wanna partyyyy!” Lyrically, Olamide weaves sharp street-smart Yoruba flows with rhythmic cadences, reflecting on hustle, leisure, and local vibes over high-energy production. Olamide holding a saxophone on the courtyard set of his Burukutu music video. Photo Credit: Styling The Stars With Swazzi/Instagram The accompanying music video directed by TG Omori matches the song’s intense cultural weight visually. It cuts dynamically between a monochromatic, glowing red corridor—where Olamide appears sharply tailored in a double-breasted suit, dark sunglasses, and dreadlocks—and an earthen-toned, arched outdoor courtyard filled with rhythmic background dancers in structured white outfits, pillbox hats, and pearl details, alongside striking scenes of Olamide stepping up to play the saxophone. Alongside the release of “Burukutu,” Olamide surprised fans by announcing the official title of his forthcoming studio project: Time & Space. Marking another milestone in his legendary discography, Time & Space is officially scheduled to drop on November 16, 2026, proving yet again why the icon remains at the very heartbeat of African music. Watch the video below The post Olamide Wants Us to Party on “Burukutu” | Watch Video appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: NASA Conducts RS-25 Engine Test in Support of Future Artemis Missions
item.description: 2 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) NASA conducts a hot fire of RS-25 engine No. 10001 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, on Oct. 21, 2026. NASA/Danny Nowlin NASA conducts a hot fire of RS-25 engine No. 10001 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, on Oct. 21, 2026. NASA/Danny Nowlin NASA conducts a hot fire of RS-25 engine No. 10001 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi, on Oct. 21, 2026. NASA/Danny Nowlin NASA tested RS-25 engine No. 10001 on Oct. 21 on the Fred Haise Test Stand at NASA’s Stennis Space Center near Bay St. Louis, Mississippi. Test teams fired the developmental engine for almost eight-and-a-half minutes (500 seconds), the same amount of time RS-25 engines fire during launch of NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket. During the test, operators also fired the engine up to the 111% power level, matching the thrust needed for new production engines to launch the SLS rocket and the Orion spacecraft to orbit. The main objectives of the test were to acceptance test RS-25 flight components for future Artemis missions and validate the new thermal protection system, which protects the RS-25 engine nozzle from the thermal environment surrounding SLS during launch. While this developmental engine will not be used in flight, the hot fire test provides NASA and NASA’s prime contractor L3Harris Technologies with the capability to capture critical data to improve engine performance and reliability. Four RS-25 engines produce up to 2 million pounds of combined thrust to help launch the SLS rocket for each Artemis mission. All RS-25 engines are tested and proven flightworthy at NASA Stennis prior to use. Tests are conducted by a team of operators from NASA, L3Harris, and Nova Space Solutions. Learn More About Artemis

item.title: OpenClaw creator says he spent $10 million in tokens last month
item.description: Peter Steinberger, member of technical staff at OpenAI and the creator of OpenClaw, estimates that he spent around $10 million in tokens running AI workloads last month. But don't feel bad for him, because it's all coming out of investors' pockets. He made this admission at the Cloudflare Connect 2026 conference in San Francisco on Wednesday, in a conversation with Cloudflare CTO Dane Knecht. Knecht previously observed that Steinberger has acknowledged having "a virtually unlimited token budget, which not all of us in the room have." Responding to the audible surprise rising from the audience, Steinberger added, "What people don't always understand is not all of that is useful." That only amplified the murmuring, perhaps not the effect he had been after. Meanwhile, his employer, OpenAI, is reportedly trying to " accelerate funding " ahead of rival Anthropic's expected IPO. Steinberger's subsequent musing about his preferred way of working failed to recognize Knecht's acknowledgement of financial limitations. "I feel like the main challenge a lot of people still have is that our infrastructure structure hasn't really caught up yet," Steinberger said. "Like why is this still using my computer? Shouldn't this all be in the cloud?" Apart from the privacy and compliance implications of relying on cloud-based AI, cost remains a consideration for anyone not setting venture funds alight. Cloud-hosted agents can be expensive. Shouldn't this all run locally? Pointing to the OpenClaw project and how a lot of open source maintainers have given up accepting pull requests due to frustration with AI slop, Knecht asked Steinberger whether we're approaching the death of open source or a golden age of AI. Steinberger said he thinks the way pull requests are handled needs to change because people don't explain how they arrived at their proposed changed code. "If I see your thoughts, how you got from A to B, my trust in the output is way higher than if you just throw the finished work across the fence," he said. Knecht also asked Steinberger whether everyone in the room would have hundreds of AI agents running in a few years. Steinberger doubts it will be hundreds. "I think everyone will have some sort of intelligence that runs and thinks and helps them throughout the day or even predicts what could help you in the future," he said. "So instead of asking the question, maybe you already get the answer." Toward the end of the session, Knecht raised the issue of trust and how to know what data to give to an agent. That's a hard question, Steinberger admitted. Part of it, he said, has to do with how much you trust the underlying model itself, because so much of model behavior is not governed by the harness – the code that wraps the model. "A lot of decisions that I built into OpenClaw early on now can change because the models are so much better," he said. Knecht previously observed that Steinberger has acknowledged having "a virtually unlimited token budget, which not all of us in the room have." Responding to the audible surprise rising from the audience, Steinberger added, "What people don't always understand is not all of that is useful." That only amplified the murmuring, perhaps not the effect he had been after. Meanwhile, his employer, OpenAI, is reportedly trying to " accelerate funding " ahead of rival Anthropic's expected IPO. Steinberger's subsequent musing about his preferred way of working failed to recognize Knecht's acknowledgement of financial limitations. "I feel like the main challenge a lot of people still have is that our infrastructure structure hasn't really caught up yet," Steinberger said. "Like why is this still using my computer? Shouldn't this all be in the cloud?" Apart from the privacy and compliance implications of relying on cloud-based AI, cost remains a consideration for anyone not setting venture funds alight. Cloud-hosted agents can be expensive. Shouldn't this all run locally? Pointing to the OpenClaw project and how a lot of open source maintainers have given up accepting pull requests due to frustration with AI slop, Knecht asked Steinberger whether we're approaching the death of open source or a golden age of AI. Steinberger said he thinks the way pull requests are handled needs to change because people don't explain how they arrived at their proposed changed code. "If I see your thoughts, how you got from A to B, my trust in the output is way higher than if you just throw the finished work across the fence," he said. Knecht also asked Steinberger whether everyone in the room would have hundreds of AI agents running in a few years. Steinberger doubts it will be hundreds. "I think everyone will have some sort of intelligence that runs and thinks and helps them throughout the day or even predicts what could help you in the future," he said. "So instead of asking the question, maybe you already get the answer." Toward the end of the session, Knecht raised the issue of trust and how to know what data to give to an agent. That's a hard question, Steinberger admitted. Part of it, he said, has to do with how much you trust the underlying model itself, because so much of model behavior is not governed by the harness – the code that wraps the model. "A lot of decisions that I built into OpenClaw early on now can change because the models are so much better," he said. Even if risks like prompt injection have been reduced through engineering efforts, Steinberger said, "you might not want to give your agent all the permissions." Instead, he suggested using an agent to authorize your agent. "You want to have another agent that can give it permissions or not and then this agent has to negotiate with another agent," he said. "Many times the agents are like, 'oh yeah, actually maybe I shouldn't do this,' or 'there's a simpler way that keeps it within the guardrails.' So those those two systems combined greatly increase my trust that I just can let the agent rip." ®

item.title: Reach new heights of laziness by burning tokens to let an AI tap your smartphone screen for you
item.description: Why use your smartphone when AI can do it for you? We’ve reached a new level of AI inanity with the launch of Opposable , a tool that taps, swipes, and types on Android phones and controls iPhones through a companion computer, sparing users the apparent burden of operating their own devices. If you don't want to update a calendar event, start a timer, or enable dark mode, you can apparently use an AI agent app on your computer (any client that supports MCP will do) to have Opposable do the thing for you on a connected phone. You could just do it on your computer, of course, but that’d require actually using your hands - like it’s some sort of baby’s toy . Lame. Opposable describes the purpose of its app as being to “give your AI thumbs” that allow an agent to open apps, read the screen, tap, and type, all while signed in to a device as the person too lazy to use a super-convenient technology themselves. As described in a blog post published by its creators Wednesday, Opposable's developers explain that its Android implementation uses accessibility services to inspect the screen, while screenshots provide visual input for an AI model. The model then decodes the images and figures out where it needs to tap on the screen in order to do whatever its user asked of it. The visual processing is handled by a vision-language model known as GUI-Owl 1.5 2B, running through llama.cpp, while tasks can be handled by either a paired desktop AI agent or an on-device agent that works without a desktop connection (the latter is available only on Android devices – iPhones require a companion computer, with a Mac beta available and a hardware-assisted Windows/Linux option also advertised). Even then, AI isn’t used for everything, with around 40 common tasks (setting an alarm, sending a text, switching Wi-Fi on or off) running as fixed code without an AI model involved. Opposable doesn’t appear to be particularly fast, however, and its accuracy is questionable too. Opposable’s website includes three different examples of tasks executed using its product, and none seem to merit using an AI over, you know, human hands. In one example, Claude Code over MCP is used to change the system’s theme to dark mode and then set a five-minute timer. This takes 50 seconds and requires 17 tool calls. In a second example using Claude Code and MCP, Opposable is asked to look up when Apollo 11 launched and who was on board, which takes just shy of two minutes. The number of tool calls isn’t mentioned, but the run cost is $0.44, which seems ridiculous when you can use your hands and figure it out for free. Hell, just asking Gemini or Siri right on a smartphone would return the answer faster and cheaper. Those half-a-buck requests to Opposable could add up pretty quickly if you’re lazy enough to justify its use. A third example shows a virtual Android device operating without a paired desktop agent, instead relying on the on-device agent that Opposable installs on Android phones. Opening
item.dc:creator: Brandon Vigliarolo
item.content:encoded: Why use your smartphone when AI can do it for you? We’ve reached a new level of AI inanity with the launch of Opposable , a tool that taps, swipes, and types on Android phones and controls iPhones through a companion computer, sparing users the apparent burden of operating their own devices. If you don't want to update a calendar event, start a timer, or enable dark mode, you can apparently use an AI agent app on your computer (any client that supports MCP will do) to have Opposable do the thing for you on a connected phone. You could just do it on your computer, of course, but that’d require actually using your hands - like it’s some sort of baby’s toy . Lame. Opposable describes the purpose of its app as being to “give your AI thumbs” that allow an agent to open apps, read the screen, tap, and type, all while signed in to a device as the person too lazy to use a super-convenient technology themselves. As described in a blog post published by its creators Wednesday, Opposable's developers explain that its Android implementation uses accessibility services to inspect the screen, while screenshots provide visual input for an AI model. The model then decodes the images and figures out where it needs to tap on the screen in order to do whatever its user asked of it. The visual processing is handled by a vision-language model known as GUI-Owl 1.5 2B, running through llama.cpp, while tasks can be handled by either a paired desktop AI agent or an on-device agent that works without a desktop connection (the latter is available only on Android devices – iPhones require a companion computer, with a Mac beta available and a hardware-assisted Windows/Linux option also advertised). Even then, AI isn’t used for everything, with around 40 common tasks (setting an alarm, sending a text, switching Wi-Fi on or off) running as fixed code without an AI model involved. Opposable doesn’t appear to be particularly fast, however, and its accuracy is questionable too. Opposable’s website includes three different examples of tasks executed using its product, and none seem to merit using an AI over, you know, human hands. In one example, Claude Code over MCP is used to change the system’s theme to dark mode and then set a five-minute timer. This takes 50 seconds and requires 17 tool calls. In a second example using Claude Code and MCP, Opposable is asked to look up when Apollo 11 launched and who was on board, which takes just shy of two minutes. The number of tool calls isn’t mentioned, but the run cost is $0.44, which seems ridiculous when you can use your hands and figure it out for free. Hell, just asking Gemini or Siri right on a smartphone would return the answer faster and cheaper. Those half-a-buck requests to Opposable could add up pretty quickly if you’re lazy enough to justify its use. A third example shows a virtual Android device operating without a paired desktop agent, instead relying on the on-device agent that Opposable installs on Android phones. Opening the clock app and switching to the stopwatch tab takes it about 96 seconds, which is supposed to be impressive, apparently, as the company behind Opposable decided to showcase it on the thing’s website. As for Opposable’s ability to actually accomplish tasks, well, that’s not exactly a sure thing. “On eight tasks the model had never been tuned on, run on the emulator twice each, giving it the whole task succeeded 4 and 3 times,” the blog post notes. I’m pretty sure my brain and hands can do better without burning tokens to fail. “Giving it one subgoal at a time and checking each claimed success against the accessibility tree before the next subgoal succeeded 6 times in both rounds,” the blog continues - so even when it gets babysat each step of the way, it still only succeeds at three-quarters of tasks. Cool - that’s really going to free up all that time wasted setting timers and doing other mundane tasks on my handset. Why someone would install this on their Android device - which requires sideloading an APK and manually granting access to read and interact with the screen through accessibility settings - seems like a bit of a mystery. Opposable’s website even warns that it could be a security disaster: “whoever holds the token can operate the phone, so treat it like a password,” but still invites users to try. An argument could be made for using Opposable as an accessibility tool for people with difficulty using a smartphone, but this isn’t mentioned anywhere on its website. Opposable is instead billed as a way to “hand off the phone chores,” leaving users free to do something else - just not on the phone currently being slowly controlled by a clumsy AI. Sure, you could give your AI some virtual thumbs through Opposable, but … why? We reached out to the Opposable team to get an answer to that question, but didn’t hear back. ® UPDATED AT 03:25 UTC, OCTOBER 2026 to add that Opposable does not consider its product an accessibility tool. "We do not market it as an assistive tool, because we have not built it or tested it as one," a spokesperson told The Reg by email. "If people with disabilities find it useful, we want to hear from them and build for them." The spokesperson also explained why demos are so slow: "It shows our small model on the Android emulator, on a laptop CPU, with no help from the phone's hardware." When running on phone, Opposable apparently does rather better. However the outfit admits it has done only very limited testing, but is about to do more.

item.title: Osas Ighodaro Looks Like a Work of Art in This Blue Mosaic Gown by House of Marvee
item.description: Osas Ighodaro standing in her custom thermal-mapped blue mosaic gown by House of Marvee. If these photos of Osas Ighodaro have you staring at your screen a little longer than usual, we completely understand. Because how do you look at a dress this beautiful and simply scroll past? The colours, the design, the way it sits on her body! There’s so much to admire, and we’re right there with you. The Nigerian-American actor, host and producer has given us many reasons to love her fashion choices over the years, but this particular look has us especially curious about how it was made. Dressed in a gorgeous blue mosaic gown by House of Marvee, Osas looks like she stepped straight out of an art exhibition. And once you hear the inspiration behind the dress, you might appreciate it even more. Actor and host Osas Ighodaro wearing a blue mosaic gown crafted from hand-painted mother-of-pearl by House of Marvee. Here’s where it gets interesting. House of Marvee drew inspiration from thermal mapping, using different shades of blue to follow the natural curves of the body. The floor-length gown features hand-painted mother-of-pearl details, creating a mosaic effect that moves between deep ocean blues and brighter turquoise tones. Look closely, and you’ll notice how the colours and textures work together across the fabric. Osas Ighodaro posing in an asymmetrical one-shoulder blue mosaic dress featuring hand-painted mother-of-pearl tiles by House of Marvee. We also love how the one-shoulder design gives the dress room to shine. One arm is covered in a long sleeve, while the other shoulder is left bare, creating a lovely contrast. Osas keeps her accessories simple with gold hoop earrings, allowing the beautiful details of the gown to remain the focus. Osas Ighodaro posing in a House of Marvee hand-painted mother-of-pearl blue gown with gold hoop earrings and a finge And can we talk about her beauty look for a second? The retro finger waves, warm-toned makeup and gold hoop earrings complement those gorgeous shades of blue beautifully. From the hand-painted details to the way the gown follows her silhouette, House of Marvee has given us a dress we’d happily spend a few more minutes admiring. Osas Ighodaro lying down in a custom House of Marvee floor-length blue mosaic dress inside an art gallery space *** Photo Credit: House of Marvee/Instagram The post Osas Ighodaro Looks Like a Work of Art in This Blue Mosaic Gown by House of Marvee appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .
